festive

/FES-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Festive means suited to a celebration, with the joyful and lively atmosphere of one.

Strings of red lanterns and drumming in the square gave the whole street a festive glow for the new year.

Example

The overnight ferry to the islands is usually a quiet ride of dozing commuters. But on the night of the solstice run, the crew strings fairy lights along the rails, an accordion player sets up near the snack bar, and passengers pass around tins of ginger cookies with strangers. Same boat, same route — but for one night the whole crossing turns festive.

The lights, live music, and shared cookies transform an ordinary crossing into one with a joyful, celebration-ready atmosphere — which is precisely what festive describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

merry: Merry means cheerful and full of good spirits -- it describes people and their mood: merry guests, a merry laugh. Festive belongs to the setting: the lights, music, and decorations that make a place feel dressed for a party. Merry people can sit in a plain room; a festive room can even be empty.

jolly: Jolly means happily good-humored, and it nearly always describes a person -- a jolly host, a jolly grandfather with a booming laugh. Festive describes places, gatherings, and atmospheres suited to celebration. People are jolly; kitchens, markets, and street fairs are festive.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gloomy: dark and cheerless

funereal: grimly solemn, like a funeral

Where it sits · how strongly the atmosphere radiates joy

pleasant → festive → exuberant

pleasant vs. festive: Pleasant describes any agreeable atmosphere; festive means the air itself feels dressed for a celebration.

exuberant vs. festive: Exuberant is stronger than festive — the joy is not just in the decorations and mood but overflowing from the people themselves.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fest: feast, holiday (Latin festum)

Suffix — -ive: having the quality of

Put it together: Festive comes straight from Latin festum, 'feast or holiday' — the root that also throws festival, fiesta, and feast itself. Add -ive, 'having the quality of,' and festive means 'having the quality of a feast day': lights up, music on, the ordinary rules of a gray afternoon suspended.

Use the root in a new word: festival: Every October the town's harvest festival takes over three streets by the river.

Word Choice

warm, everyday; describes atmospheres, decor, and moods

Festive describes a joyful, holiday-like atmosphere and doesn't need an actual occasion — a kitchen can feel festive on any random Tuesday — while celebratory (also in this unit) always points at a specific event being marked, like a win or a milestone.
